verdict: OK to lend in Alang shipbreaking/ship-repair, but only to yards with EU-list or EU-ready compliance and to repair-linked cash flows; avoid sub-scale beaching-only yards with no compliance spend.
title: Alang shipbuilding & repair: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**Alang is the world's largest shipbreaking cluster, and the cash engine is dismantling steel, not building hulls.** A yard buys an end-of-life vessel, beaches it, cuts it into plate and scrap over weeks, and sells to re-rollers and mills; the ship-repair and conversion work is the higher-margin, faster-turn side. Alang is in Gujarat, the biggest demolition hub globally [1]. **Value sits in the buy price of the vessel and the speed of cutting, not in the yard's fixed assets** — land is leased, the capex is cutting equipment and compliance infrastructure, so the real asset is the plot and the licence to operate.

## Where cash sits and what has changed
**Working capital is inventory-heavy and lumpy: one vessel is a single large cash outlay that converts to scrap sales over the cutting cycle.** So when a proposal lands, check the vessel-wise stock statement and the age of unsold inventory; if a yard is holding cut plate beyond its normal selling cycle, ask why and price the inventory at realisable scrap value, not book. **The live change is the EU vote on 4 November on adding Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers to the EU authorised list** [1] — that is the single event that re-rates a yard's access to European-flag tonnage. Note the source is a trade-press report dated 29-30 October 2026, so treat the outcome as pending. **Local reporting in August 2026 described recession clouds over Alang with 38 ships arriving in four months** [3] — that is the local demand picture, and it is softer than the national print.

## The growth opportunity
**National shipbuilding and repair output is running hot — IIP NIC 30 up 25.3% YoY and 22.7% Apr-to-date** [D] — and Gujarat GST is growing 11.9% versus India's 6.1% [D], so the state's trade is expanding faster than the country. **Peer evidence says repair is where the margin is: Cochin Shipyard's repair segment grew 157.2% YoY at 59% of revenue with 22.6% EBITDA, while shipbuilding EBIT was 8.3%** [4]. Pursue Alang yards with a repair/conversion order book and EU-list or EU-ready compliance spend; avoid pure beaching yards with no environmental capex and no repair capability. **Peer guidance also warns margins normalise — Cochin guided FY27 EBITDA to about 14% from 24% in FY26, with repair at 22-24% and shipbuilding at 10-12%** [5][6]. So do not underwrite a yard at peak repair margins.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the vessel, not the balance sheet: sanction a vessel-specific facility with the scrap-sale receivables escrowed to us.** Take monthly stock-and-cut reports, vessel-wise purchase and sale invoices, and a compliance certificate on hazardous-waste handling. **Bank credit nationally is growing 27.0% against output of 22.7%, a 4.3 pp gap** [D] — so the sector is being lent to faster than it produces; insist on our own yard-level discipline rather than riding the tide.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the EU vote outcome and any delay past 4 November** [1] — a rejection closes European tonnage to these two yards and hits their pipeline. **Watch monthly vessel arrivals and cutting days; the August local report of 38 ships in four months** [3] is the base to beat. **Watch inventory age and scrap-price realisation** — a yard sitting on unsold plate is a yard with a cash problem.
